tagline: Andes, oil, and the world's tallest waterfall
overview:
Venezuela occupies the northern edge of South America, with a long Caribbean coastline and borders with Colombia, Brazil and Guyana. At about 916,000 km² it is roughly twice the size of California, and it contains snow-capped Andean peaks, tropical grasslands, the Orinoco River delta and a corner of the Amazon rainforest.

About 28 million people live in Venezuela, speaking Spanish along with more than thirty Indigenous languages. Caracas, the capital, sits in a narrow valley just inland from the Caribbean, hemmed in by a steep green mountain called Ávila.

Venezuela is a presidential republic. It holds the largest proven oil reserves of any country, which once made it among the richest in Latin America. Since around 2014 it has experienced a severe economic and political crisis: extreme inflation, shortages of food and medicine, disputed elections, and the departure of more than seven million people, one of the largest movements of people in the world.
landAndNature: The Andes reach into western Venezuela, topping out at Pico Bolívar at about 4,978 meters. North of the Orinoco spread the llanos, vast seasonal grasslands that flood in the wet season and dry to hard earth in the dry, home to capybaras, anacondas, caimans and the scarlet ibis. South and east lies the Guiana Shield, where flat-topped mountains called tepuis rise sheer from the forest, their summits isolated for millions of years so that unique plants grow there. From one of them, Auyán-tepui, Angel Falls drops 979 meters, the tallest uninterrupted waterfall on Earth. Over Lake Maracaibo, lightning flashes hundreds of nights a year in a phenomenon called the Catatumbo lightning, among the most frequent anywhere.
peopleAndCulture: Venezuelan food centers on corn: arepas, split and stuffed with cheese, beans or shredded beef, are eaten at any meal, and hallacas, corn dough parcels steamed in banana leaves, are made by families together at Christmas. Baseball is the leading sport, and Venezuela has sent many players to the major leagues; soccer has grown fast. Joropo, a swift music of harp, four-stringed cuatro and maracas, comes from the llanos. El Sistema, a program founded in 1975, has given free classical music training to hundreds of thousands of children and produced the conductor Gustavo Dudamel. Beauty pageants are followed with unusual enthusiasm, and Venezuela has won Miss Universe many times.
history: Indigenous peoples including the Carib, Arawak and Timoto-Cuica lived here when Columbus reached the coast in 1498; a later explorer called the stilt villages on Lake Maracaibo 'little Venice', which gave the country its name. Spanish rule lasted three centuries. Simón Bolívar, born in Caracas, led the fight that freed Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from Spain, and Venezuela became fully independent in 1830 after the union he founded broke apart. Civil wars and strongmen filled the 1800s. Oil discovered around Lake Maracaibo in the 1920s transformed the country, which became a stable democracy from 1958. Hugo Chávez was elected president in 1998 and used oil money for social programs; after his death in 2013 and a collapse in oil prices, the country entered a deep crisis under Nicolás Maduro.
funFacts: Angel Falls plunges 979 meters, so far that much of the water turns to mist before reaching the bottom.
The Catatumbo lightning over Lake Maracaibo flashes on more nights per year than almost anywhere else on Earth.
Venezuela's tepuis are flat-topped mountains that inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's novel The Lost World.
El Sistema has taught free classical music to hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan children since 1975.
Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves of any country, much of it heavy crude near the Orinoco River.
